doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Learning to improvise before theory; Dad's ballad and Mike Lorenz lessons
summary: Ries improvised to capture the feeling he saw in his father, then a neighbor showed him chords from a fake book and professor Mike Lorenz taught improvisation.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well I was just thinking that now, because I’m wondering if you learned how to improvise before you had any theoretical basis for what you were doing?

I did. And just I think to capture mostly that feeling of seeing him, because I had an older brother who died and he was the oldest and I was the youngest. So I often wonder if, me having three children, I can’t imagine that happening. So I wonder also if that was his going into that other world or something. But I just — he was very different at the piano than — on the trumpet he was like beautiful sound, amazing tone. In fact I remember as a little kid being on one of his gigs, and it was a dance gig. And he always had three, four, five hundred people, there was huge amounts of people. And what would often be the case with that period is like people would go hear musicians play and then you know you’d see people dancing and then they would get close to the bandstand and they would just watch the band, and they would kind of hear whoever was taking a solo or something. And my dad wasn’t a heavy improviser but one of the most beautiful tones and just singing through the instrument. And I remember this young couple, maybe in their twenties and maybe they were going to get married or something but they were dancing in the front. And they stopped in front of the stage and were watching my father play. And he was playing a melody to a ballad. And I remember both of them started crying. And I thought to myself my dad just playing a melody made somebody cry. So I think before the notes and how, without impressing anybody with your technique just the idea that music really can capture this heavy emotional, you know, seeing him going into that place on the piano but also then channeling that on the trumpet too. So you know and then a neighbor who also played the trumpet, and I was starting trying to like how do I improvise, how do I do this. And I saw these fake books with the music. And he came over and he played the trumpet but they also could play piano. And he sat down and it was like looked at the fake book and it was like I said, “How are you doing that?” He goes, “Oh this is super easy. This is the bass note, I just play the bass note on the left, bass and fifth and seventh and this is the root.” I’m like, “That’s it?” He goes, “Yeah.” Then it was like a whole new world. Like oh now I can start figuring out these chords.” And then there was a university near my house, my dad took me to that, and I met with this professor in high school and he started scheduling improvisation lessons, and he played the organ and piano and trumpet and trombone, and he was a very musical guy named Mike Lorenz. He was great. And that was it. It was kind of like opening the door to like now, I get the theoretical idea of it plus I know the emotional aspect of it that like
now theoretically what is this chord, how do you do that, and then to dissect the chord and then I started composing.
